model.label: Tax-funded, residence-based national health service: the state owns most hospitals and primary care centres and Icelandic Health Insurance (Sjúkratryggingar Íslands) is the single national purchaser, with monthly caps on user charges and a stepped co-payment scheme for medicines

overview.statement: Iceland's health system rests on universal, tax-funded coverage under highly centralised governance: entitlement depends on residence, and Icelandic Health Insurance (Sjúkratryggingar Íslands, SÍ) covers almost everyone and is the only national purchaser of services.
Care is delivered through seven health districts in a mainly public system: primary care centres and hospitals are state-owned, so the state is both the main owner of providers and the main payer.

In recent years SÍ has increasingly contracted private outpatient specialist clinics; temporary regulations, extended through May 2026, allow it to reimburse self-employed specialists so that care continues and backlogs shrink.

As of the 2023 country profile, most primary care was delivered by public health centres and every hospital was public; several proposals for private hospitals made over the previous decade had not been carried out.
Public health insurance covers people once they have been legally resident in Iceland for six months in a row.
Care is heavily concentrated in the Reykjavík area: Landspítali, the national hospital, performs most complex inpatient care, and most private specialist capacity is also in the capital region.

First- and second-generation immigrants made up 18% of Iceland's population in 2022, up from about 8% in 2012, and the 2023 profile says that overcoming language barriers and offering culturally sensitive services remains a central topic of discussion.

financing.statement: Health care is paid for mainly out of general government revenue and covers all legal residents; the government is both payer and owner of most providers, and policy, administration and financing are run nationally rather than locally.
Primary care, whether delivered by public or private centres, is paid for from general taxation; public centres have long dominated the sector.

Using the OECD System of Health Accounts definition (government and compulsory schemes), public funding paid for 83.6% of current health spending in 2023, above the EU average of 80.0%, and out-of-pocket payments made up 14.7% of total spending, slightly below the EU average.
Out-of-pocket spending consists mostly of co-payments for primary care, outpatient specialist care and medicines, with reduced charges or exemptions for vulnerable groups.
Private sources paid for 16.4% of health spending in 2023 (EU average 20%): 14.7% came straight from households as out-of-pocket payments and only 1.7% from voluntary insurance.
Voluntary health insurance funds less than 2% of health spending and is bought mainly by newly arrived residents who are not yet eligible for public cover.
Real health spending per person rose 7% from 2019, almost all of it publicly funded; out-of-pocket spending per person grew only 1.8% between 2019 and 2023.
Outpatient care from private specialists is a significant part of the system, and the government reimburses about 75% of the cost of private-sector health care (2023 profile).

covered.statement: Iceland covers practically the whole population with a broad benefit package; financial protection comes from monthly caps on user charges for covered services and a stepped co-payment scale for outpatient medicines with an annual cap, set lower for children, pensioners and people with disabilities.
Public sources paid for 99% of hospital costs and 84% of outpatient care spending in 2023, a higher share for outpatient care than the EU average.

Only 34% of dental spending was publicly financed in 2023, roughly the EU average; children under 18 get basic dental care fully covered for an annual fee of ISK 3,500, and pensioners and people with chronic conditions had about 69% of general dental costs covered.
In June 2024 Iceland Health and the Icelandic Dental Association signed a five-year agreement guaranteeing public payment toward dental care for children, older people and people with disabilities.
In the year before June 2024, 62,883 children received dental care paid for by Iceland Health, which covers all necessary dental treatment for children apart from an entry fee.

covered.statement: Charges that count toward the monthly payment cap include health centre fees, hospital day-ward and outpatient fees, self-employed specialist doctors, diagnostic tests and imaging, bone density scans, some dermatology light treatment, children's psychological services under the framework agreement with psychologists, physiotherapy, occupational therapy and speech therapy.
Since autumn 2023 free HPV vaccination has also been offered to boys under a gender-neutral policy.

A population-based colorectal cancer screening programme started in 2025, inviting people aged 60 to 74 for a faecal immunochemical test every two years, with results sent through the Heilsuvera health portal.

Decisions on which medicines are reimbursed are made by the Icelandic Medicines Agency on the basis of an expert review by the Landspítali Medicine Committee, which weighs each product's clinical benefit, cost-effectiveness and likely budget impact.

Iceland does not carry out its own health technology assessments; the Medicines Agency uses other Nordic countries' assessments, and since 2024 Iceland has taken part in the Joint Nordic HTA project, which shares methods and knowledge on new medicines.
Iceland Health must approve in advance before it pays toward cataract surgery, light therapy for skin conditions and specified plastic surgery.

cost_sharing.statement: Iceland Health caps what a person pays for covered health services each month; the full maximum is ISK 37,794 for most adults and ISK 25,198 for older people, disabled people, people on a rehabilitation pension and children aged 2-18, while children under 2 pay nothing.

cost_sharing.statement: All children in one family count as a single child under the payment cap.

cost_sharing.statement: The cap rebuilds over time: for a general-rate adult it starts from ISK 6,299 and rises by ISK 6,299 for each month without health care use, up to the full ISK 37,794.

For outpatient medicines, patients pay the full price until their costs over a rolling 12 months reach ISK 22,800 (about EUR 160), then 15% up to ISK 32,430, then 7.5% up to ISK 62,000 (about EUR 433); above that, public insurance pays everything.
Public insurance paid only 41% of retail pharmaceutical spending in 2023 (EU average 62%), so medicines made up 45% of all out-of-pocket spending, almost twice the EU average of 25%.

Patient charges for medicines are tied to a reference price: a patient who picks a more expensive alternative pays the whole price difference, and that extra does not count toward the annual co-payment cap.

Under a 2019 plan to lower financial barriers, the fee for a daytime GP visit was cut by nearly a third in 2021 to ISK 500 (about EUR 3.50), while the specialist visit fee stayed at ISK 3,400 (about EUR 23) despite inflation.

Since 2024 'soft gatekeeping' guidance expects specialist care normally to begin with a family doctor's referral for the visit to be reimbursed, and patients pay lower co-payments for referred specialist visits.
From 1 July 2025 children seeing a specialist doctor without a referral no longer pay 30% of the bill, although referrals are still required for physiotherapy and speech therapy.
Since late 2023 public insurance has shared the cost of semaglutide for weight management, but only under strict criteria.

financial_hardship.statement: Even with lower charges and caps for children, pensioners and people with disabilities, the 2025 country profile finds that the high initial deductibles for medicines weigh more heavily on Icelandic households than in most European countries.

additional_care.statement: Voluntary health insurance is the main source of cover for people who have lived in Iceland for less than six months and do not yet qualify for public insurance.

The number and scope of private (non-profit and for-profit) clinicians has grown faster than the number of doctors overall in recent years, a pattern the 2023 profile describes as roughly in line with EU trends.
Most private specialist clinics are located in the capital area, where about two thirds of the population lives.
A 2017 primary care reform, aimed at better availability and quality, brought in a new reimbursement model, and two new privately run primary care centres opened after a public tender.

access.statement: Only 13% of Icelandic doctors work as GPs (EU average 19%), or 0.6 GPs per 1,000 people versus 0.8 in the EU, and an estimated half of residents had no fixed family doctor in late 2023.

Iceland had 15.2 nurses per 1,000 people in 2023, counting registered and licensed practical nurses, the second-highest density in Europe, and its doctor-to-population ratio is also above the EU average.

A 2016 plan aimed for 80% of elective surgery patients to be treated within 90 days, but backlogs persisted and grew during COVID-19: in 2022 more than 80% of joint-replacement patients and 69% of cataract patients waited longer than 90 days.

Hip and knee replacement waits fell sharply after targeted funding, pay-per-case incentives and the purchase of 700 extra operations from private providers: a record 2,138 operations were done in 2023 and the median wait at Landspítali fell from 9.5 to 4.6 months.

Cataract surgery waits have grown: Landspítali's waiting list reached 3,000 people by August 2023, 1,000 of them waiting more than a year, and in 2024 78% of patients waited longer than 90 days, the highest share on record.

In 2020 over 91% of residents could reach a hospital with round-the-clock surgery and overnight care within 30 minutes by car, and 99.5% lived within a 30-minute drive of some health service, counting 47 primary care centres and 22 part-time sites.
Iceland has one official helicopter emergency medical services base, at Akureyri, which can meet up to 66% of demand within 60 minutes.

By 2024 more than half of adults were active users of Heilsuvera, the national health portal for booking appointments, viewing results, renewing prescriptions and video consultations, with strong use in every region.
Iceland had 2.6 hospital beds per 1,000 people in 2023, about half the EU average, and hospital discharge rates were 32% below the EU average.

A 2025 National Audit Office review found that Landspítali, the main hospital, could not fill its 2024 staffing plan: 50 registered nurse and 379 licensed practical nurse posts were vacant, which limited surgery and added pressure on high-dependency wards and emergency rooms.

Iceland had about 2,800 nursing-home beds at the end of 2023 and 677 people on the waiting list in June 2025, delaying hospital discharges; about 100 more places a year are needed to 2040, and 1,041 new beds are planned for 2025-2029.
In 2021 average waits for mental health services were more than four months for children and nearly six months for adults, though they varied widely by type of service.
New medicines reached the Icelandic market a median of 513 days after EU authorisation in 2020-2023, close to the EU median of 518 days.

In a national cohort surveyed between December 2020 and July 2021, people with a history of psychiatric disorders or chronic physical conditions were more likely to report that their health care had been disrupted during the pandemic.

outcomes.statement: Life expectancy at birth was 82.8 years in 2024, more than a year above the EU average, but still 0.4 years below its 2019 level after a 1.1-year fall in 2022 when COVID-19 deaths rose.
In 2024 a 30-year-old man without secondary education could expect to live 5.1 years less than a university-educated man of the same age; for women the gap was 4.2 years.
Preventable mortality was 125 deaths per 100,000 people in 2022, 26% below the EU average.
Over the last decade treatable mortality (deaths under 75 avoidable through health care) has stayed at about 60 per 100,000, roughly a third below the EU average.
In the GBD 2019 study, Iceland's Healthcare Access and Quality (HAQ) Index score for ages 0-74 was 93.1 (95% uncertainty interval 91.3-94.4) in 2019, 15.2 points higher than in 1990.

outcomes.statement: Hospital admissions for chronic conditions that good primary care can usually prevent were, taken together, a third below the EU average in 2023, and diabetes admissions were 71% lower.

In the OECD PaRIS survey of 2023-24, only about a third of Icelandic patients with chronic conditions felt confident managing their health or reported well-coordinated care, far below the 60% EU average.
Fewer than half of patients with three or more chronic conditions had a medication review in the past year, well below the EU average.

In 2024, 97% of young children had a first measles vaccine dose (EU 92%), and 93% of 15-year-old girls were vaccinated against HPV, the second-highest rate in Europe and about 30 percentage points above the EU average.
In 2023, 62% of eligible women took part in cervical cancer screening and 56% in breast cancer screening, against EU averages of 58%.

In two rural nurse-led diabetes clinics in North Iceland (88 patients, 2019-2020), about 70% of type 2 diabetes patients met the clinical target for HbA1c at follow-up, 56% for systolic and 49% for diastolic blood pressure, and 33% for body mass index.
The share of adults who smoke daily fell from 22% in 2003 to under 6% in 2023, the lowest rate in Europe.

costs.statement: Health spending was EUR 3,905 per person in 2023 (adjusted for purchasing power), 1.9% above the EU average, but only 8.7% of GDP against 10.0% in the EU.
Inpatient and outpatient care each took about 31% of health spending in 2023, together more than 60%, and each about 3 percentage points above the EU share.
Long-term care took 19% of health spending in 2023 (EU 18%), medicines and medical devices under 15% (EU 18%), and prevention just 2%, half the EU share.
Preliminary 2024 data show total health spending per person rising by nearly 5% on the previous year.
Retail spending on medicines was EUR 480 per person in 2023, 6% below the EU average but the highest among the Nordic countries, about 16% above their average.

Medicine prices are capped by reference to Denmark, Finland, Norway and Sweden: most prescription medicines may not exceed the average Nordic wholesale price, and high-cost specialty medicines are capped at the lowest price in the region.

In the first year of the 2017 reimbursement model in the Reykjavík area, total reimbursements, reimbursements per GP, registered patients and cost per visit did not differ significantly between public and private primary care centres.

what_works.statement: The 2025 country profile reports that Iceland has some of the lowest avoidable mortality rates in Europe and takes this as evidence of effective public health and health care.

The 2025 profile attributes the fall in joint-replacement waits to targeted purchasing, performance-linked funding and focused management attention after a national waiting-times dashboard was introduced.
The 2025 profile credits Iceland's low diabetes hospitalisation mainly to strong nurse-led primary care, while noting that the disease is also less common there.
More than 80% of antibiotics prescribed in Iceland are from the WHO 'Access' group, well above the 65% target.

By automating appointment booking and prescription requests, the Heilsuvera portal has reduced clinical staff workload, and secure messaging and online consultations increasingly replace in-person visits for non-urgent problems.

With pharmacists paid extra for dispensing the cheapest product (or one within 5% of it), generics made up 49% of the medicines market by volume in 2021, similar to the EU average, above Sweden (37%) and below Denmark (69%).
Iceland trains twice as many nurses each year as the EU average, counting both registered and licensed practical nurse programmes.
People infected with COVID-19 did not report more disruption to their health care than others, which the authors take as a sign that the system kept services accessible to them during the pandemic.

problems.statement: GP density fell by 0.3% a year over the past decade, while it rose by more than 1% a year on average in the EU.

Hospital bed occupancy routinely exceeds the 85% safety threshold, and staff shortages, which the National Audit Office identified as the main bottleneck, are causing emergency department crowding, postponed elective operations and fewer usable beds.
Ministry of Health projections say the hospital system will need about 50% more beds by 2040 than are planned for 2026.
As of January 2025 only 31% of medicines approved in the EU were available to patients in Iceland, against 46% on average across the EU; for cancer medicines the figures were 34% and 50%.
No nursing home meets the safe-staffing benchmark of at least 60% registered nurses, partly because funding limits hiring and training.

When she abolished the children's referral requirement in 2025, the Minister of Health said the referral system had led poorer families' children, who needed referrals for financial reasons, to wait longer for care than children whose parents could pay to see a specialist without one.
In 2019, 22% of Icelandic adults were obese, compared with 15% in the EU.
Investment in health information technology quadrupled in 2023, yet at EUR 0.8 million per 100,000 people it was still 65% below the EU average.
In 2019 about 20% of men and women in the lowest income fifth reported depression, against 6.7% of men and 9.4% of women in the highest fifth.

reforms.statement: In August 2025 the government announced a multi-year plan to buy about 1,000 extra elective operations a year through long-term contracts.
In June 2025 Minister of Health Alma D. Möller abolished the referral requirement for children seeing specialist doctors (and related tests), effective 1 July 2025.
The National Action Plan on antimicrobial resistance for 2025-2029 aims to cut antibiotic use by a further 20% from 2022 levels by 2029.
In 2024 doctors and pharmacists moved to a 36-hour working week on condition that productivity was maintained, at a time of growing workforce pressure.
Medical school intake rose from 48 in 2019 to 75 in 2024, and since 2023 every new doctor must complete a one-year foundation internship before specialising.
To ease the GP shortage the government has expanded family medicine training and raised the maximum working age for doctors outside hospitals from 70 to 75.

Major hospital construction is under way: the building shell was completed in late 2024, interior work began in June 2025 and completion is scheduled for around the end of 2027, while groundwork for an expansion of Akureyri Hospital in the north is expected in summer 2026.
The government proposed a long-term obesity strategy in 2024, and since January 2025 primary-school lunches have been free nationwide.
In 2021 oversight of cancer screening moved from the Icelandic Cancer Society to the public sector, with a new national screening centre coordinating programmes and public providers delivering them.
